prompt:
Write an essay of about 1,500 words on whether primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting. Take a side and argue for it.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Write mostly medium-length, complete sentences.

text:
Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting, and they should teach it with more confidence rather than less. The case against it has grown louder as keyboards and tablets have spread through classrooms, and it rests on an appealing idea: that cursive is a relic, like slide rules and shorthand, and that the hours spent on it would be better used elsewhere. I think that argument misreads what handwriting is for, overstates what screens can replace, and underestimates what a child gains from learning to write fluently by hand.

Begin with the plainest fact, which is that people still write by hand throughout their lives. They sign forms, fill in notes, label boxes, scribble shopping lists, annotate documents and take quick notes in meetings where a laptop would feel intrusive. Pupils sit examinations with a pen in their hand for years after they leave primary school, and in many countries the written paper remains the dominant form of assessment at sixteen and eighteen. A child who cannot write quickly and legibly is at a real disadvantage in those moments, and the disadvantage is not trivial. Examiners cannot reward answers they cannot read, and a pupil who must labour over each letter has less attention left for the argument they are trying to make. Handwriting is a tool, and the sensible response to a tool that people will keep needing is to teach it properly.

The strongest reason to teach joined-up writing in particular is speed combined with legibility. Printing each letter separately forces the pen to lift after every character, and that lifting costs time. A joined script lets the hand move in a continuous flow, so the writer can keep pace with their own thoughts. Many teachers have seen what happens to children who are never taught to join their letters. Some develop a slow, laboured print that tires the hand, and others invent a private and often untidy hybrid with no consistent logic. The aim of teaching a joined style is not to produce decorative calligraphy. It is to give every child a efficient and readable method before bad habits set in, so that handwriting becomes automatic and stops demanding effort.

That automaticity matters because of what it frees up. Cognitive scientists have long described the problem of limited working memory, which is the small mental workspace we use to hold ideas while we shape them into sentences. When a young writer must consciously think about how to form each letter, the effort consumes part of that workspace, and there is less left over for spelling, grammar, vocabulary and the shape of the whole piece. Research with primary pupils has repeatedly found that children whose handwriting is fluent tend to write longer and better compositions than those whose handwriting is still a struggle. The causal story is plausible and fairly intuitive. Once the motor skill becomes effortless, the mind can attend to meaning. Teaching a fluent joined hand is therefore not a distraction from composition but one of the ways schools help children compose.

There is also a growing body of evidence that writing by hand does something for learning that typing does not quite replicate. Studies in neuroscience and psychology have compared children and adults who learn letters by writing them with those who learn them by typing or tracing, and several have found stronger and more widespread brain activity in the handwriting groups, along with better letter recognition. Other work suggests that students who take notes by hand often process the material more deeply, because they cannot transcribe everything and so must decide what matters. I would not want to lean too heavily on any single study, since this field contains plenty of small samples and contested results, and some of the headline findings on note-taking have been hard to reproduce. Even so, the direction of the evidence is consistent enough to give the sceptic pause. Nobody has shown that abandoning handwriting improves a young child's thinking, and there are reasonable grounds to suspect it might do harm.

The objection I take most seriously is that time in the primary curriculum is limited, and that every hour given to handwriting is an hour taken from reading, mathematics, science or learning to type. This is a fair point, but it assumes the trade-off is larger than it is. Handwriting practice is usually brief and frequent, a matter of ten or fifteen minutes here and there, and it can be woven into spelling and composition rather than treated as a separate subject. Typing, moreover, is not an alternative to handwriting but a complement to it. Children can and should learn both, and there is no evidence that doing so overloads them. A school that can teach a nine-year-old to read, add, draw and play a recorder can surely find the time to teach the same child to join their letters.

A second objection is that cursive is hard and that insisting on it penalises children with difficulties such as dyspraxia or dysgraphia. Here the answer is not to abandon the script but to teach it well and to be flexible about the exceptions. Some children with significant motor difficulties will always do better with a keyboard, and schools should give them one without fuss or stigma. That is an argument for reasonable adjustment, not for removing the skill from the many children who can master it. It is also worth noting that some specialists consider a joined, flowing script easier for certain struggling writers than print, because it removes the awkward question of where each letter starts and stops and reduces the reversals that trouble children who confuse letters such as b and d. The experience is mixed, which is a reason for teachers to use judgement, not a reason to drop the practice.

A third objection is cultural rather than practical, and it says that cursive is simply old-fashioned and that schools exist to prepare children for the future, not to preserve the past. I find this argument weaker than it first appears. Schools preserve many things that are old because they remain useful, and nobody proposes dropping long division merely because calculators exist. Handwriting also carries a modest but real human value. A handwritten letter, a birthday card or a note left on a kitchen table communicates something that typed text does not, and it is a skill that people are often glad to have. Historians and archivists, meanwhile, point out that a generation who cannot read cursive will be cut off from letters, diaries and documents written by their own grandparents. That loss would arrive quietly and could not easily be reversed.

It is worth being honest about the limits of my argument. Joined-up writing is not magic, and the quality of the teaching matters far more than the style chosen. A child who is drilled joylessly through pages of looped letters will gain little, and some countries and schools have wasted effort on elaborate scripts that look beautiful on a wall but are not used by anyone in adult life. The best approach is probably a simple, consistent, lightly joined style, taught early and practised regularly, which children can later adapt into a personal hand that suits them. Perfection is not the goal. Fluency, legibility and comfort are.

Nor should anyone pretend the policy debate is purely about evidence. Several American states abandoned cursive teaching under the Common Core standards and later restored it, partly in response to parents and teachers who felt something valuable had been lost. Some Nordic countries moved decisively towards keyboards, and then began to reconsider after concern about falling literacy and weaker handwriting. These swings suggest that the case for dropping handwriting was made with more enthusiasm than evidence, and that the costs became visible only after the change. Education has a long record of discarding useful practices in pursuit of novelty and then rediscovering them at some expense. We should be cautious about repeating that cycle with a skill whose benefits are well supported and whose costs are small.

When all this is weighed together, the case for keeping joined-up handwriting in primary schools is strong. It equips children with a fast, legible and durable way to record their thoughts. It frees mental capacity for the harder work of composing ideas. It may support learning and memory in ways that typing does not match. It costs little time, it can be adapted for children who struggle, and it preserves a connection to written culture that would be hard to rebuild. Keyboards are indispensable and every child should learn to use one, but they do not make the pen obsolete. Schools should teach both, and they should teach the pen first and with care, because the habits formed in those early years last a lifetime. A child who writes confidently by hand has been given something practical, something cognitive and something quietly personal, and that is worth the few minutes a day it takes to teach.
